claim: Learning can occur without external feedback.
source: It is well established that learning can occur without external feedback, yet normative reinforcement learning theories have difficulties explaining such instances of learning.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Normative reinforcement learning theories have difficulties explaining instances of learning without external feedback.
source: It is well established that learning can occur without external feedback, yet normative reinforcement learning theories have difficulties explaining such instances of learning.
evidence: Stated as a known limitation in the abstract

claim: Human observers are capable of generating their own feedback signals by monitoring internal decision variables.
source: Here, we propose that human observers are capable of generating their own feedback signals by monitoring internal decision variables.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors

claim: Mesolimbic brain areas encode both anticipation and prediction error of confidence.
source: we found that mesolimbic brain areas encoded both anticipation and prediction error of confidence—in remarkable similarity to previous findings for external reward-based feedback.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis presented in the study

claim: The mesolimbic confidence prediction error modulation predicts individual learning success.
source: we demonstrate that the model accounts for choice and confidence reports and show that the mesolimbic confidence prediction error modulation derived through the model predicts individual learning success.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between striatal CPE signal and learning success

claim: Reinforcement learning models depend on feedback from the environment.
source: The behavioral changes arising from learning have quite successfully been described by the reinforcement learning principle (Sutton and Barto, 1998), according to which biological agents continuously adapt their behavior based on the consequences of their actions. Thus, reinforcement learning models and most other learning models depend on feedback from the environment.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with citation to Sutton and Barto, 1998

claim: Perceptual learning has been demonstrated to occur without feedback.
source: Such perceptual learning has repeatedly been demonstrated to occur without feedback (Herzog and Fahle, 1997; Gibson and Gibson, 1955; McKee and Westheimer, 1978; Karni and Sagi, 1991)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Previous work has emphasized the role of reinforcement learning in perceptual learning.
source: Previous work has emphasized the role of reinforcement learning in perceptual learning (Kahnt et al., 2011; Law and Gold, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Previous reinforcement learning accounts of perceptual learning were based on external feedback and cannot account for learning without external feedback.
source: However, these accounts were based on perceptual learning with external feedback and therefore cannot account for instances in which learning occurs without external feedback.
evidence: Logical inference from the limitations of previous models

claim: In the absence of external feedback, learning is guided by internal feedback processes that evaluate current perceptual information in relation to prior knowledge about the sensory world.
source: Here, we pursued the idea that, in the absence of external feedback, learning is guided by internal feedback processes that evaluate current perceptual information in relation to prior knowledge about the sensory world.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested in the study

claim: Introspective reports of perceptual confidence could serve as a window into internal feedback processes.
source: We reasoned that introspective reports of perceptual confidence could serve as a window into such internal feedback processes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors

claim: Low or high confidence corresponds to a negative or positive self-evaluation of one's own perceptual performance, respectively.
source: In this scenario, low or high confidence would correspond to a negative or positive self-evaluation of one's own perceptual performance, respectively.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the model

claim: Confidence could act as a teaching signal in the same way as external feedback in normative theories of reinforcement learning.
source: Accordingly, confidence could act as a teaching signal in the same way as external feedback in normative theories of reinforcement learning (Daniel and Pollmann, 2012; Hebart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous work

claim: A confidence-based reinforcement signal could strengthen neural circuitry that gave rise to high-confidence percepts and weaken circuitry that led to low-confidence percepts.
source: Applied to the case of perceptual learning, a confidence-based reinforcement signal could serve to strengthen neural circuitry that gave rise to high-confidence percepts and weaken circuitry that led to low-confidence percepts, thereby enhancing the quality of future percepts.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors

claim: 29 participants completed the study.
source: Human participants (N=29) learned to detect the orientation of peripheral noise-embedded Gabor patches relative to a horizontal or vertical reference axis while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample

claim: The experiment comprised four sessions: an initial behavioral test session, an intensive perceptual learning session in the MRI scanner, and two behavioral post-training test sessions.
source: Overall, the experiment comprised four sessions: (i) an initial behavioral test session to establish participants' baseline contrast thresholds for a performance level of 80.35% correct responses, (ii) an intensive perceptual learning session (training) in the MRI scanner with a continuous threshold determination, and two behavioral post-training test sessions to examine (iii) short-term and (iv) long-term stimulus-specific training effects (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design

claim: Participants did not receive external cognitive or rewarding feedback during the entire experiment.
source: Importantly, participants did not receive external cognitive or rewarding feedback during the entire experiment.
evidence: This is a key feature of the experimental design

claim: Participants reported their confidence about the stimulus orientation on a visual analogue scale.
source: Rather, in addition to their choice, they reported their confidence about the stimulus orientation on a visual analogue scale (for a verification of accurate usage, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure

claim: Contrast thresholds improved for the trained reference axis.
source: The contrast thresholds improved for the trained (t28 = 6.73, p < 0.001, two-tailed), but not for the untrained reference axis (t28 = 0.41, p = 0.68; interaction of training × time: F1,28 = 14.2, p < 0.001), demonstrating clear and specific effects of perceptual learning.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Contrast thresholds did not improve for the untrained reference axis.
source: The contrast thresholds improved for the trained (t28 = 6.73, p < 0.001, two-tailed), but not for the untrained reference axis (t28 = 0.41, p = 0.68; interaction of training × time: F1,28 = 14.2, p < 0.001), demonstrating clear and specific effects of perceptual learning.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Stimulus-specific training effects could be detected 10 weeks later.
source: These stimulus-specific training effects could still be detected 10 weeks later (F1,28 = 4.3, p = 0.047), indicating long-term stability and thus demonstrating a key characteristic of perceptual learning (Karni and Sagi, 1993).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data at long-term follow-up

claim: Contrast threshold consistently decreased across runs during the training session.
source: The analysis showed that contrast threshold consistently decreased across runs (linear slope: −0.006 ± 0.002, t28 = −2.38, p = 0.024), from 8.64% ± 0.47 (mean ± SEM) in the first training run to 7.68% ± 0.52 in the last training run.
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis of behavioral data

claim: Performance increased monotonically with confidence.
source: The performance increased monotonically with confidence (main effect of percentile: F22,2442 = 5.76, p < 0.001, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures), approaching chance at low levels of confidence, without showing ceiling effects at high levels of confidence (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between confidence and performance

claim: Confidence represents valuable self-generated feedback.
source: This pattern indicates a close link between the decisional certainty of the choice and the reported confidence and shows that confidence represents valuable self-generated feedback.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed relationship between confidence and performance

claim: The model assumes that observers improve perceptual performance by optimizing a filter on incoming sensory evidence.
source: Our model assumes that observers improve perceptual performance by optimizing a filter on incoming sensory evidence.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture

claim: The filter is represented by signal weights and noise weights connecting orientation energy detectors to decision units.
source: The filter is represented by two components: signal weights for clockwise (cw) and counterclockwise (ccw) stimulus orientation (wccw,ccw; wcw,cw), connecting orientation energy detectors Eccw/cw to decision units Accw/cw with same orientations; and noise weights (wccw,cw; wcw,ccw), connecting detectors Eccw/cw to decision units Acw/ccw with opposing orientations.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture

claim: Perceptual learning is based on an associative reinforcement learning rule with a reinforcement component and a Hebbian component.
source: Finally, perceptual learning is based on an associative reinforcement learning rule with two separate components: a reinforcement component utilizes a confidence prediction error (CPE; denoted as δ) as internal feedback, representing the mismatch between current confidence and a long-term estimate of expected confidence (via a learning rate αc); and a Hebbian component ensures that the weights are updated in proportion to how strongly orientation detectors and decision units co-activate.
evidence: This is a description of the model learning rule

claim: The energy content was higher for the spatial frequency and orientations used to generate the Gabor patches relative to other frequencies and orientations.
source: As expected, the energy content was higher for the spatial frequency and orientations used to generate the Gabor patches relative to other frequencies and orientations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This validates the representational subsystem of the model

claim: The energy for designated orientations was higher for correct than for incorrect responses.
source: Further, when orientation energy was computed separately for correct and incorrect responses, the energy for designated orientations (i.e., the orientations used to generate the Gabor patches) was higher for correct than for incorrect responses (t28 = 8.1, p < 0.001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of orientation energy

claim: The energy for opposite orientations was lower for correct than for incorrect responses.
source: whereas the energy for opposite orientations (i.e., ∓20° if ±20° was presented) was lower for correct than for incorrect responses (t28 = −3.6, p = 0.001) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of orientation energy

claim: The varying orientation energy was directly associated with behavior.
source: This pattern demonstrated that the varying orientation energy was directly associated with behavior and adds to the validation of the model.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between orientation energy and behavioral responses

claim: The model accounted well for participants' choices.
source: This analysis showed that the model accounted well for participants' choices (mean ± SE of individual z-transformed correlation coefficients: rPearson = 0.64 ± 0.03; one-sample t-test against Fisher z' = 0: t28 = 26.2, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between model predictions and actual choices

claim: The model could predict participants' trial-wise confidence reports.
source: A correlation between the model-based decisional certainty and participants' confidence reports confirmed that confidence, too, was captured by the model (mean ± SE of rPearson = 0.32 ± 0.02, t28 = 15.4, p < 0.001; Figure 4B; see Figure 4—figure supplement 3 for single-subject data).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between model predictions and actual confidence reports

claim: Signal weights increased linearly across runs.
source: As depicted in Figure 4C, we found a linear increase for signal weights across runs (mean ± SEM of slope = 0.0147 ± 0.0036, t28 = 4.1, p < 0.001)
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis of model-derived signal weights

claim: Noise weights decreased linearly across runs.
source: and a linear decrease for noise weights (slope = −0.0036 ± 0.0010, t28 = −3.5, p = 0.001).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis of model-derived noise weights

claim: Individual contrast threshold learning slopes correlated negatively with the slopes of signal weights.
source: Furthermore, the individual contrast threshold learning slopes correlated negatively with the slopes of signal weights (rPearson = −0.45, p = 0.013)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between behavioral and model-derived measures

claim: Individual contrast threshold learning slopes correlated positively with the slopes of noise weights.
source: and positively with the slopes of noise weights (rPearson = 0.46, p = 0.011).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between behavioral and model-derived measures

claim: Individual learning was well captured by the signal and noise weights of the model.
source: Thus, individual learning was well captured by the signal and noise weights of the model.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlations between learning slopes and weight changes

claim: Striatal activation reflects a positive anticipatory response at the beginning of a trial and a subsequent prediction error response related to the outcome.
source: The results of these previous studies suggest that striatal activation reflects a positive anticipatory response at the beginning of a trial as well as a subsequent prediction error response related to the outcome.
evidence: This is based on previous reward-based learning studies

claim: The BOLD time courses exhibited a first peak 4-6 s after trial onset, consistent with an anticipatory confidence signal.
source: Specifically, 4–6 s after trial onset (reflecting the hemodynamic delay), the BOLD time courses exhibited a first peak, consistent with an anticipatory confidence signal at the start of a trial
evidence: Supported by analysis of event-related BOLD time courses

claim: The BOLD time courses displayed a positive deflection for high-confidence trials and a negative deflection for low-confidence trials 4-6 s after stimulus onset.
source: 4–6 s after stimulus onset, the BOLD time courses displayed a positive deflection for high-confidence trials and a negative deflection for low-confidence trials.
evidence: Supported by analysis of event-related BOLD time courses

claim: There was above-baseline striatal activation at trial onset, indicative of an anticipatory signal.
source: A statistical analysis confirmed above-baseline striatal activation at trial onset, indicative of an anticipatory signal (left peak at [−10 14 −6], t28 = 6.42, prFWE < 0.001; right peak at [12 14 −8], t28 = 7.78, prFWE < 0.001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: There was a main effect of confidence at stimulus onset in the bilateral ventral striatum.
source: as well as a main effect of confidence at stimulus onset in the bilateral ventral striatum (left peak at [−10 14 −4], t28 = 10.56, prFWE < 0.001; right peak at [16 12 −8], t28 = 11.46, prFWE < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Reinforcement based on reward and based on confidence share a common neural substrate both in the anticipation and the outcome period.
source: This model-free assessment provides initial support for the idea that reinforcement based on reward and based on confidence share a common neural substrate both in the anticipation and the outcome period.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of neural patterns to reward-based studies

claim: There was a significant parametric modulation of striatal activation by expected confidence at trial onset.
source: As conjectured, we found a significant parametric modulation of striatal activation by expected confidence at trial onset (right peak at [8 14 −4], t28 = 4.12, prFWE = 0.018; left peak at [−12 20 −2], t28 = 3.97, prFWE = 0.026; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by model-based fMRI analysis

claim: Striatal activation at trial onset reflects anticipated confidence for the upcoming stimulus presentation.
source: This model-based result corroborates the notion that striatal activation at trial onset reflects anticipated confidence for the upcoming stimulus presentation, analogous to previous findings of an anticipatory reward signal in the ventral striatum (Delgado et al., 2000; Preuschoff et al., 2006; Knutson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference from the model-based fMRI results and comparison to previous studies

claim: The bilateral ventral striatum showed a strong positive relationship with the confidence prediction error.
source: As hypothesized, the bilateral ventral striatum showed a strong positive relationship with the CPE (left peak at [−16 8 −10], t28 = 7.64, prFWE < 0.001; right peak at [16 14 −8], t28 = 7.81, prFWE < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by model-based fMRI analysis

claim: The ventral tegmental area showed modulation by confidence prediction error.
source: This modulation was also present in our second region of interest, the ventral tegmental area (peak at [−6 −22 −16], t28 = 3.02, prFWE=0.027; see Supplementary file 2 for a whole-brain list of active brain regions).
evidence: Supported by model-based fMRI analysis

claim: The CPE was represented by the same key brain structures that have been implicated in signaling reward prediction errors.
source: In sum, the CPE was represented by the same key brain structures that have been implicated in signaling reward prediction errors (Schultz et al., 1997; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Berns et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference from the fMRI results and comparison to previous reward studies

claim: Orientation energy was encoded in left occipital cortex.
source: We found that OE was encoded in left occipital cortex (peak at [−44 70 0], t28 = 4.77, pcFWE = 0.033), an area overlapping with voxels activated by the stimulus localizer (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by multivariate fMRI analysis

claim: Decision value was encoded in right middle frontal gyrus.
source: Instead, we found significant encoding of the DV in right middle frontal gyrus (peak at [32 14 44], t28 = 5.87, pFWE = 0.026; Figure 6B), in line with a recent report (Hebart et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multivariate fMRI analysis and consistent with previous findings

claim: Perceptual and decision variables of the model can be mapped to visual and frontal cortex, respectively.
source: Thus, perceptual and decision variables of our model can be mapped to visual and frontal cortex, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference from the multivariate fMRI results

claim: There was a significant relationship between the striatal CPE signal and individual perceptual learning success in the left ventral striatum.
source: As hypothesized, we found a significant relationship between the striatal CPE signal and individual perceptual learning success in the left ventral striatum (rPearson = 0.400, p = 0.016, one-tailed; without age correction: rPearson = 0.37, p = 0.026)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between fMRI signal and behavioral learning index

claim: There was a trend for a relationship between the striatal CPE signal and individual perceptual learning success in the right ventral striatum.
source: and a trend in the right ventral striatum (rPearson = 0.268, p = 0.080; without age correction: rPearson = 0.24, p = 0.11) (see Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between fMRI signal and behavioral learning index

claim: The result is congruent with a viable role of CPE-based feedback signals for perceptual learning in the absence of external feedback.
source: This result is congruent with a viable role of CPE-based feedback signals for perceptual learning in the absence of external feedback.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between CPE signal and learning success

claim: Mesolimbic confidence signals mirror those typically found for reward, both in the anticipation period and for prediction errors.
source: In support of this view, our model-free fMRI analyses revealed that mesolimbic confidence signals mirror those typically found for reward, both in the anticipation period (Preuschoff et al., 2006; Delgado et al., 2000; Knutson et al., 2001) and for prediction errors (Schultz et al., 1997; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Berns et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings with comparison to previous reward studies

claim: The model successfully described the learning process as a continuous adjustment of a perceptual filter linking sensory and decision units.
source: The model successfully described the learning process as a continuous adjustment of a perceptual filter linking sensory and decision units.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's performance

claim: The strength of the striatal modulation by CPEs predicted participants' perceptual improvements.
source: Importantly, the strength of the striatal modulation by CPEs predicted participants' perceptual improvements, further corroborating the behavioral relevance of these internally-generated feedback signals.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis between CPE signal and learning success

claim: The observed pattern of confidence-related activity in the mesolimbic system fits well with the prediction error hypothesis of dopamine.
source: The observed pattern of confidence-related activity in the mesolimbic system, including the co-modulation of the ventral tegmental area, fit well with the prediction error hypothesis of dopamine, which posits that dopaminergic midbrain neurons and their targets respond at two time points during a learning trial (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of the dopamine prediction error hypothesis

claim: The same principle that holds for reward could hold for confidence: participants learn to anticipate a certain level of confidence for the upcoming trial based on past confidence experiences.
source: Here, we argue that the same principle could hold for confidence: participants learn to anticipate a certain level of confidence for the upcoming trial based on past confidence experiences, and this anticipatory state is activated when the beginning of a new trial is indicated (equivalent to a cue).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the results

claim: A modulation of striatal activity by expected confidence at trial onsets was found, as previously reported for expected reward.
source: In congruence with this postulation, we indeed found a modulation of striatal activity by expected confidence at trial onsets—as previously reported for expected reward (Preuschoff et al., 2006; Delgado et al., 2000; Knutson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings with comparison to previous reward studies

claim: In the confidence domain, the outcome corresponds to the level of confidence calculated from the stimulus and the prediction error is computed as the difference between expected confidence and actual confidence.
source: In the confidence domain, the outcome would correspond to the level of confidence calculated from the stimulus and the prediction error would be computed as the difference between expected confidence and actual confidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of how confidence fits into the prediction error framework

claim: Self-generated confidence assumes the role of external reward in dopaminergic prediction-error-based reinforcement learning when no external feedback is available.
source: Overall, our results may therefore indicate that self-generated confidence assumes the role of external reward in dopaminergic prediction-error-based reinforcement learning when no external feedback is available.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the results

claim: A previous fMRI study by Kahnt and colleagues investigated perceptual learning with external reward and found that behavioral improvements were well explained by a reinforcement learning model.
source: In particular, an fMRI study by Kahnt and colleagues (Kahnt et al., 2011) investigated perceptual learning with external reward and found that behavioral improvements were well explained by a reinforcement learning model.
evidence: This is a summary of a previous study

claim: The previous study by Kahnt and colleagues reported stimulus information encoded in visual cortex and model-derived decision value in frontal cortices, in agreement with the findings of the present study.
source: Their results exhibit a notable parallel to the present findings: the authors reported stimulus information encoded in visual cortex and model-derived decision value in frontal cortices, in agreement with the findings of the present study.
evidence: This is a comparison of the present results to a previous study

claim: The previous study by Kahnt and colleagues identified a perceptual learning-related reward prediction error in the ventral striatum, dovetailing with the finding of a perceptual learning-related confidence prediction error in the same brain region in the present study.
source: In addition, this previous study identified a perceptual learning-related reward prediction error in the ventral striatum, dovetailing with our finding of a perceptual learning-related confidence prediction error in the same brain region.
evidence: This is a comparison of the present results to a previous study

claim: The combined Hebbian and reinforcement learning model extends previous models by implementing confidence prediction errors in replacement of reward prediction errors.
source: Importantly, our combined Hebbian and reinforcement learning model extends and improves previous models in several ways. First and foremost, by implementing confidence prediction errors in replacement of reward prediction errors, it extends previous reward reinforcement learning models of perceptual learning (Law and Gold, 2009; Kahnt et al., 2011) to cases without feedback.
evidence: This is a description of how the present model improves upon previous models

claim: Previous models based on a single 'readout weight' have the limitation that negative prediction errors reduce the readout weight, which leads to an additional reduction in performance.
source: Second, these previous models were based on the assumption that perceptual performance is determined by a single 'readout weight', representing the amplification of stimulus information in sensory areas. While the simplicity of these models is appealing, they are limited in the sense that negative prediction errors have an unreasonable influence on behavior: according to these models, worse-than-expected feedback reduces the readout weight, which leads to an additional reduction in performance.
evidence: This is a critique of previous models

claim: The associative reinforcement learning rule of the present model entails a behaviorally advantageous function of negative prediction errors: inhibition of sensory noise.
source: By contrast, the associative reinforcement learning rule of the present model entails a behaviorally advantageous and plausible function of negative prediction errors: inhibition of sensory noise.
evidence: This is a description of an advantage of the present model

claim: A conceptually related reinforcement learning model for perceptual categorization implies that stimuli exclusively activate the correct stimulus category, an assumption that disregards the ambiguity of incoming stimulus information.
source: Third, a conceptually related reinforcement learning model for perceptual categorization (Daniel and Pollmann, 2012) implies that stimuli exclusively activate the correct stimulus category, an assumption that disregards the fact that the ambiguity of incoming stimulus information is an essential property of perceptually demanding tasks.
evidence: This is a critique of a previous model

claim: The present model utilizes a dedicated representational subsystem to estimate the activation of all implemented input units, and their differential activity determines perceptual choices.
source: In contrast, the present model utilizes a dedicated representational subsystem (Petrov et al., 2005) to estimate the activation of all implemented input units, and it is their differential activity that determines perceptual choices.
evidence: This is a description of an advantage of the present model

claim: The associative reinforcement learning rule in the model was inspired by the three-factor learning rule, which has been proposed to underlie the potentiation of synapses in the striatum.
source: The associative reinforcement learning rule in the model was inspired by the three-factor learning rule (Schultz, 2002; Reynolds et al., 2001), which has been proposed to underlie the potentiation of synapses in the striatum.
evidence: This is a description of the biological plausibility of the model

claim: The three-factor learning rule proposes that changes in neural transmission in cortico-striatal synapses depend on coincident presynaptic and postsynaptic activity (Hebbian learning) and on the presence of dopamine error signals.
source: It proposes that changes in neural transmission in cortico-striatal synapses not only depend on coincident presynaptic and postsynaptic activity (Hebbian learning), but also on the presence of dopamine error signals.
evidence: This is a description of the three-factor learning rule

claim: Ashby and colleagues have suggested that the basal ganglia are a key region for learning in perceptual tasks.
source: Indeed, Ashby and colleagues (Ashby et al., 2007; Hélie et al., 2015) have previously suggested that the basal ganglia, which represent the predominant site of dopaminergic synaptic plasticity, are themselves a key region for learning in perceptual tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of previous theoretical work

claim: Ashby and colleagues proposed that the basal ganglia serve to activate the appropriate target regions in executive frontal cortices shortly after sensory cortex activation.
source: They proposed that (i) the basal ganglia serve to activate the appropriate target regions in executive frontal cortices shortly after sensory cortex activation
evidence: This is a summary of previous theoretical work

claim: Ashby and colleagues proposed that basal ganglia learning is superseded by cortico-cortical Hebbian learning, once the correct cortico-cortical synapses are built.
source: and (ii) such basal ganglia learning is superseded by cortico-cortical Hebbian learning, once the correct cortico-cortical synapses are built.
evidence: This is a summary of previous theoretical work

claim: The account by Ashby and colleagues fits well with the present model, in which perceptual learning corresponds to the process of reweighting connections between sensory and decisional units.
source: This account fits well with the present model, in which perceptual learning corresponds to the process of reweighting connections between sensory and decisional units.
evidence: This is a comparison of the present model to previous theoretical work

claim: The optimization of perceptual read-out could be mediated via reinforcement learning in the basal ganglia.
source: These considerations in combination with the present results thus lend support to the hypothesis that the optimization of perceptual read-out (as implicated by our model) could be mediated via reinforcement learning in the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the present results and previous theoretical work

claim: Thirty healthy, right-handed female participants took part in the experiment.
source: Thirty healthy, right-handed female participants took part in the experiment in return for payment after giving written informed consent.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample

claim: One participant was excluded due to fixation failure, leaving 29 valid participants.
source: One participant was excluded due to fixation failure, leaving 29 valid participants (24.1 ± 2.5 years, range 19–31 years).
evidence: This is a description of the final participant sample

claim: Participants of only one gender were selected because male and female brains on average have different brain volumes, introducing between-subject noise in the spatial normalization procedure.
source: Participants of only one gender were selected in view of the planned between-subject analysis, because male and female brains on average have different brain volumes (Ruigrok et al., 2014), introducing between-subject noise in the spatial normalization procedure
evidence: This is a justification for the participant selection criteria

claim: Male and female brains have slightly different hemodynamic response profiles, which could impact the detectable BOLD signal.
source: and slightly different hemodynamic response profiles (Jaušovec and Jaušovec, 2010), which could impact the detectable BOLD signal.
evidence: This is a justification for the participant selection criteria

claim: The study was conducted according to the declaration of Helsinki, and approved by the ethics committee of the Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin.
source: The present study was conducted according to the declaration of Helsinki, and approved by the ethics committee of the Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance

claim: The training session took place in an fMRI scanner with a back-projection screen setup.
source: The training session took place in an fMRI scanner with a back-projection screen setup (Sanyo PLC-XT21L, 60 Hz, resolution 1024 x 768).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup

claim: The pre- and post-test took place around one week before and one day after the training session, respectively.
source: Around one week (7.1 ± 0.2 days) before and one day after the training session, the behavioral pre- and post-test took place in a darkened room
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline

claim: A long-term test was conducted around 10 weeks after the training session.
source: Around 10 weeks (70.6 ± 2.1 days) after the training session, a long-term test was conducted with a setup identical to the pre- and post-test sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline

claim: Each trial started with a fixation screen for 2000 ms ± 1000 ms, followed by the presentation of the stimulus for 100 ms.
source: Each trial started with a fixation screen for 2000 ms ± 1000 ms, followed by the presentation of the stimulus for 100 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the trial structure

claim: Participants reported their confidence prior to reporting their choice to avoid a potential bias by the choice itself.
source: To avoid a potential bias by the choice itself (Kvam et al., 2015; Sniezek et al., 1990; Sieck, 2003; Tafarodi et al., 1999), participants reported their confidence prior to reporting their choice.
evidence: This is a justification for the order of responses

claim: The confidence rating scale was visualized as a half-open circle that linearly increased in width and color.
source: The confidence rating scale was visualized as a half-open circle (radius r = 4° of visual angle) that linearly increased in width (0.1° to 1° visual angle) and color (black to green), whereby the orientation and angular direction of the circle changed randomly from trial to trial.
evidence: This is a description of the confidence rating interface

claim: The test sessions were divided into blocks of 16 trials with alternating reference axes.
source: The test sessions were divided into blocks of 16 trials with alternating reference axes and continued until the termination criterion of a staircase procedure was reached.
evidence: This is a description of the test session structure

claim: The staircase procedure started with a one-up-one-down staircase with a relative stepsize of 0.05 log units to rapidly approximate the rough threshold range.
source: The staircase procedure started with a one-up-one-down staircase with a relative stepsize of 0.05 log units to rapidly approximate the rough threshold range (start contrast: cp = 20%; cf. Eq. 1).
evidence: This is a description of the staircase procedure

claim: After three reversals, the algorithm switched to a weighted one-up-two-down staircase for fine-tuning.
source: After three reversals, the algorithm switched to a weighted one-up-two-down staircase (Kaernbach, 1991) for fine-tuning.
evidence: This is a description of the staircase procedure

claim: The ratio of stepsize down / stepsize up was set to 0.5488, leading to convergence at a performance of 80.35 percent correct.
source: The ratio of stepsize down / stepsize up was set to 0.5488 (García-Pérez, 1998) with stepsize down set to 0.33%, leading to convergence at a performance of 80.35 percent correct.
evidence: This is a description of the staircase procedure

claim: The training session in the fMRI scanner comprised an initial adjustment run and nine training runs, each with 48 trials.
source: The training session in the fMRI scanner comprised an initial adjustment run and nine training runs, each with 48 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the training session structure

claim: During the training session, participants viewed only one reference axis ('trained reference axis').
